deadline_label: File up to 6 months before proposed start date; cap-subject petitions keyed to April lottery window
Electronic registration window opens early March; lottery results April; H-1B start date no earlier than Oct 1
non_obvious_official_guidance: H-1B cap is 65,000 per fiscal year plus 20,000 for beneficiaries with a US master's degree or higher. Employer submits an electronic registration each March and USCIS selects petitions via random lottery among registrations.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Selection is not guaranteed — in FY2026 USCIS received approximately 470,000 registrations for 85,000 available numbers, a roughly 18% selection rate. An unselected employee cannot begin cap-subject H-1B employment and must either wait for the next lottery cycle (earliest start Oct 1 of the following fiscal year) or qualify for a cap-exempt pathway. SME HR generalists routinely underestimate this timeline risk and plan offers assuming H-1B is available on demand.
non_obvious_action_required: Assess whether employer qualifies as cap-exempt before the offer is made. If cap-subject, plan for a possible 12–18 month delay between offer and work authorization. File at every registration window without gaps. Consider O-1 or L-1 as parallel tracks; explore cap-exempt initial-placement strategies for eligible employers. Track registration status via USCIS online account immediately after the window closes.

authority: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration
deadline_label: DOL must certify LCA before USCIS petition is filed; DOL processes within 7 business days

authority: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
form_name: No form — employer-maintained physical or electronic file
deadline_label: Created on the day the H-1B petition is filed; maintained for 1 year after employment ends
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers must maintain a Public Access File at the place of employment (or principal place of business) containing the certified LCA, wage rate documentation, and evidence of LCA posting notice. The PAF must be made available to any member of the public upon request within 1 business day (20 CFR §655.760).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most SME HR teams are unaware the PAF must exist and be immediately producible on request. DOL Wage and Hour Division conducts compliance audits; civil money penalties reach $5,788 per violation per worker per day for failure to maintain or produce the file. The PAF is not submitted to any agency — it lives only at the employer's worksite — making it easy to overlook, and the first time most HR generalists learn about it is when a WHD investigator asks for it.
non_obvious_action_required: Create a PAF folder (physical or electronic) on the petition filing date. Mandatory contents: certified LCA, documentation of actual wage paid to the H-1B worker, documentation of prevailing wage determination, list of workers in the same occupational classification at the worksite, and evidence of the 10-day LCA posting (physical or electronic). Update the PAF whenever the LCA is amended or renewed. Store separately from the general personnel file and label it clearly as the H-1B Public Access File.

authority: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration
form_name: Form ETA-9141 (PWD request) via FLAG system
deadline_label: Obtain before filing the LCA; DOL-issued PWD valid 1 year from determination date

form_name: Form I-129 (cap-exempt designation noted in petition)
deadline_label: Cap-exempt petitions may be filed at any time of year — no lottery, no cap
non_obvious_official_guidance: Certain employer categories are exempt from the H-1B annual cap: institutions of higher education, nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with such institutions, nonprofit research organizations, and government research organizations (INA §214(g)(5)).
non_obvious_actual_reality: HR professionals at SMEs routinely do not know that initial H-1B employment at a cap-exempt institution can establish H-1B status that is then transferable to a cap-subject employer — bypassing the lottery entirely. Additionally, any employee who was previously counted against the H-1B cap does not re-enter the lottery when changing to a new cap-subject employer; they are already cap-counted and may transfer immediately. This cap-portability rule is almost universally unknown to first-time HR generalists and means that experienced H-1B workers with prior cap-subject approval are not subject to the April lottery.
non_obvious_action_required: Before assuming a candidate must enter the lottery, ask immigration counsel two questions: (1) Has this employee ever held H-1B status and been counted against the cap? If yes, no new lottery is required. (2) Does the employer have any affiliation with a university or research institution? If yes, explore cap-exempt filing. These two checks alone can eliminate 12–18 months of waiting for a significant portion of H-1B cases.

deadline_label: Filed concurrently with or after I-129; guaranteed USCIS action within 15 business days
File up to 6 months before start date; no cap or lottery applies
File up to 6 months before start date; no cap or lottery applies

authority: U.S. Department of State / U.S. Embassy or Consulate
deadline_label: After I-129 approval notice received; schedule consular appointment — allow 4–12 weeks for availability
Check within 24–72 hours of arrival via CBP I-94 website
non_obvious_official_guidance: CBP generates an electronic I-94 automatically when a traveler enters the US at an air or sea port of entry. The record is available at i94.cbp.dhs.gov and shows the class of admission and authorized period of stay.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The I-94 record frequently contains errors — wrong visa class (e.g., 'H-1B1' instead of 'H-1B'), wrong expiration date, or 'D/S' (Duration of Status) entered for a fixed-term worker whose petition has an explicit end date. An incorrect I-94 means the employee's status is mis-documented; any employment relying on a defective I-94 may be treated as unlawful. CBP officer data-entry errors regularly go undetected for months, only discovered at a subsequent border crossing or RFE.
non_obvious_action_required: Log in to [i94.cbp.dhs.gov/](https://i94.cbp.dhs.gov/) within 24 hours of arrival. Verify: (1) class of admission matches the visa type (e.g., H-1B); (2) admission date is correct; (3) authorized stay period matches the I-129 approval notice end date. If any field is wrong, file CBP Form I-102 or attend a local Deferred Inspection Site in person immediately — do not delay. Save and print the correct I-94 record; attach it to the employee's immigration file.

field_label: I-94 Controls Authorized Stay — Not the Visa Stamp
deadline_label: Understand immediately upon arrival; set calendar reminder for I-94 expiry
non_obvious_official_guidance: A US visa stamp in the passport authorizes travel to a US port of entry to seek admission. It does not independently authorize the period of stay or employment. The I-94 issued at entry determines the authorized period of stay and the classification under which the employee may work.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Employees routinely confuse the visa stamp expiration date with their authorized stay. A 3-year H-1B visa stamp does not mean the employee is authorized to remain until the stamp expires — the I-94 may show an earlier date. Working or remaining past I-94 expiry (even with a valid visa stamp) constitutes an immigration status violation and accrues unlawful presence, which triggers 3-year or 10-year bars to re-entry upon departure. This is one of the most common self-inflicted compliance failures for otherwise compliant H-1B workers.
non_obvious_action_required: Record the I-94 expiry date separately from the visa stamp expiry in the employee's HR calendar. Set a reminder 6 months before I-94 expiry to file an H-1B extension petition. If transitioning from F-1 OPT to H-1B, understand the cap-gap I-94 notation and what it covers. Never rely on a visa stamp date as the controlling authorization end date.

deadline_label: Apply after arrival; SSA recommends waiting 10 days post-entry for CBP records to sync

field_label: SSN Card Notation — 'Valid for Work Only with DHS Authorization'
deadline_label: Notation printed on card at issuance; employee should be briefed before the card arrives
non_obvious_official_guidance: SSA issues Social Security cards to non-immigrants who are authorized to work with a required annotation: 'VALID FOR WORK ONLY WITH DHS AUTHORIZATION.' This notation is mandated by 20 CFR §422.107(e) and does not indicate any deficiency in work authorization.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Credit bureaus, apartment rental screening agencies, background check vendors, and some financial institutions misread this notation as a flag for suspect status or restricted employment eligibility. Employees face credit application denials, failed background checks for rental housing, and bank account refusals because screeners are unfamiliar with the legally-required language. The notation is a routine government label — it does not limit the scope of authorized employment under the H-1B petition at all.
non_obvious_action_required: In the pre-arrival briefing pack, include an explicit explanation of the SSN card notation and why it appears. Provide the employee with a template response they can use when a screener flags the notation: 'This notation is required by federal regulation (20 CFR §422.107). My work authorization is evidenced by my I-129 approval notice and I-94 record.' Attach copies of the I-129 approval notice and I-94 to any background check package. For apartment applications, advise the employee to proactively show the visa and I-94 alongside the SSN card.

deadline_label: Section 1 completed by first day of employment; Section 2 completed by end of third business day
source: INA §274A; 8 CFR §274a.2; M-274 (I-9 Handbook for Employers)

authority: State Department of Motor Vehicles (varies by state)
form_name: State-specific (e.g., CA DMV DL 44; TX DL-14A)
field_label: State Driver's License or State ID Card
deadline_label: Within 10–60 days of establishing state residency (varies by state); check state DMV requirement
source: State vehicle codes (e.g., California Vehicle Code §12502; Texas Transportation Code §521.021); REAL ID Act 2005

deadline_label: REAL ID required for domestic air travel and federal building access effective May 7, 2025
non_obvious_official_guidance: The REAL ID Act (Pub. L. 109-13) requires that from May 7, 2025, only federally-issued IDs or REAL ID-compliant state driver's licenses may be used to board domestic commercial flights or access federal facilities. REAL ID-compliant cards are marked with a star in the upper right corner.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many newly arrived employees visit the DMV, obtain a standard (non-REAL ID) state license, and discover at the airport that it is stamped 'NOT FOR FEDERAL IDENTIFICATION' and rejected by TSA. Work visa holders must present additional immigration documents (I-94, I-129 approval notice) at the DMV for a REAL ID application — the appointment takes longer than a standard renewal, and some DMV staff are unfamiliar with the documentation requirements for visa holders. In several states, the license validity is limited to the immigration document expiry date.
non_obvious_action_required: Explicitly request a REAL ID-compliant card (with the star) at the initial DMV visit — it is not always the default. Required documents typically include: passport, US visa, I-94 print-out, I-129 approval notice, proof of Social Security number (or denial letter from SSA if SSN not yet issued), and two proofs of state residency. If the state ties license validity to immigration status expiry, note the expiry date in the HR file and plan to renew when the H-1B is extended.
source: REAL ID Act of 2005, Pub. L. 109-13; 49 USC §30301 note; 6 CFR Part 37

deadline_label: As soon as SSN is available (3–4 weeks post-arrival); some banks accept alternatives earlier
non_obvious_official_guidance: There is no federal law requiring an SSN to open a US bank account. However, banks must verify customer identity under the Bank Secrecy Act Customer Identification Program (31 CFR §1020.220), and most major institutions require an SSN as the preferred identifier.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Newly arrived H-1B and L-1 employees routinely spend 4–6 weeks without a US bank account because SSN cards take 3–4 weeks to arrive by mail after the SSA appointment. During this window, direct deposit enrollment is impossible, and the employer may issue paper checks. Some banks (notably Citibank, HSBC, and Chase at branch manager discretion) will open accounts for work visa holders who appear in person with: passport, visa, I-94, I-129 approval notice, and employer letter — without requiring the SSN card. Others refuse. The inability to open a bank account is a genuine practical blocker that HR teams must anticipate.
non_obvious_action_required: Research the bank's specific CIP policy before the employee arrives. Advise the employee to visit a bank branch in person — not online — with all available immigration documents. For employers with large banks as corporate partners, a relationship banker can often facilitate account opening for international employees. Once the SSN card arrives, have the employee update the account record immediately. Provide a paper check or pre-paid card option as a bridge for the first payroll cycle if direct deposit cannot be established in time.
source: Bank Secrecy Act 31 USC §5318(l); 31 CFR §1020.220 (CIP Rule)

deadline_label: Complete by first day of employment

authority: State Department of Revenue (varies by state)
form_name: Varies by state (e.g., CA DE-4; NY IT-2104; IL W-4)
deadline_label: Complete alongside federal W-4 on first day of employment
source: State income tax codes (varies); IRS Publication 15-A

authority: Internal Revenue Service / Social Security Administration
form_name: No employee form — employer withholds via payroll
deadline_label: Withheld from first paycheck; employer matches 6.2%

form_name: No employee form — employer withholds via payroll
deadline_label: Withheld from first paycheck; employer matches 1.45%
source: IRC §3101(b); IRC §3102(f) (Additional Medicare Tax); IRS Publication 15

form_name: No form — determined by immigration classification
field_label: FICA Exemption Does NOT Apply to H-1B / L-1 / O-1 Workers
deadline_label: Determine at first payroll setup; update payroll system on exact visa-change date
non_obvious_official_guidance: Nonresident aliens in F-1, J-1, M-1, or Q-1 status are exempt from FICA taxes on wages for services performed in the US while maintaining those statuses (IRC §3121(b)(19)). H-1B, L-1, O-1, and TN workers do not qualify for this exemption and are subject to full FICA from the first paycheck.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Employees transitioning from OPT (F-1 status) to H-1B commonly expect FICA exemption to continue. On October 1 — the H-1B start date — FICA withholding must begin immediately. Payroll teams at SMEs frequently miss this change, resulting in FICA under-withholding for months. The IRS can assess both employee and employer shares plus interest and penalties. The reverse error also occurs: payroll systems that correctly applied FICA during a prior H-1B stint sometimes continue withholding after an employee briefly returns to F-1 status, deducting FICA the employee is actually exempt from.
non_obvious_action_required: Create a payroll system trigger linked to visa status change dates. On the exact H-1B start date, activate FICA withholding. Brief the employee in advance — the net pay reduction (7.65% combined employee share) is a visible and often unexpected change from their OPT paychecks. Do not rely on carryover settings from the prior tax setup. If the employee is transitioning from H-1B back to OPT (rare but occurs), remove FICA withholding on the F-1 OPT start date.
source: IRC §3121(b)(19); IRS Publication 515 (Withholding of Tax on Nonresident Aliens)

deadline_label: Typically within 30 days of hire date; late enrollment requires waiting until next open enrollment
source: ERISA §601; ACA §1201; IRC §4980H (employer mandate for 50+ FTE employers)

authority: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services / Healthcare.gov
form_name: Healthcare.gov marketplace application (state exchange in some states)
field_label: ACA Marketplace Enrollment (if no employer coverage offered)
deadline_label: Special Enrollment Period triggered by arrival or loss of prior coverage — 60-day window

field_label: IRS Substantial Presence Test — US Tax Residency
deadline_label: Assessed at year-end; determines correct tax form (1040 vs 1040-NR) and worldwide income exposure
non_obvious_official_guidance: A person is a US resident for income tax purposes if they meet the Substantial Presence Test: physically present in the US for at least 31 days in the current year AND 183 days under a weighted 3-year formula (100% of current-year days + 1/3 of prior-year days + 1/6 of the year before that). Days in F/J/M/Q status as an 'exempt individual' do not count.
non_obvious_actual_reality: An employee arriving from abroad in, say, April on an H-1B may meet the SPT by late summer and become a US tax resident for the full calendar year — meaning they owe US income tax on worldwide income, including salary earned in their home country before the move. This surprises nearly every new H-1B arrival who expects to owe US tax only on US-source income. The worldwide income exposure can be substantial for executives with equity vesting or bonus structures from their home employer.
non_obvious_action_required: On arrival, calculate the employee's projected SPT count using the 3-year formula. If they will meet SPT in the arrival year, connect them immediately with a US international tax advisor — not a standard CPA. Key questions for the advisor: (1) Does the home country have a US income tax treaty with a tie-breaker provision? (2) Are there foreign tax credits to offset double taxation? (3) Is a first-year choice election (IRC §7701(b)(4)) advantageous? Do not wait until January of the following year.
source: IRC §7701(b); IRS Publication 519 (US Tax Guide for Aliens)

form_name: Form 1040 (with Form 1040-NR as attached statement for nonresident period)
field_label: Dual-Status Tax Return — Year of Arrival
deadline_label: Filed by April 15 of the year following arrival (Oct 15 with extension)
non_obvious_official_guidance: In the year an individual changes from nonresident to resident alien status, they file a dual-status return: Form 1040 covers the resident period (worldwide income) and a Form 1040-NR statement covers the nonresident period (US-source income only). The 1040-NR is attached to the 1040 as a supporting statement, not filed separately.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Consumer tax software (TurboTax standard, H&R Block basic) cannot correctly produce a dual-status return. Most general-practice CPAs are also unfamiliar with the dual-status rules. Employees who file as a pure resident or pure nonresident when dual-status applies typically either overpay or create an IRS correspondence audit. Income tax treaty benefits applicable to the nonresident period are commonly missed entirely, resulting in over-withholding that is never recovered.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a US international tax professional — specifically one with nonresident and dual-status experience — for the first US tax return. The employee should gather before the tax appointment: all non-US income documents from the pre-arrival period, W-2 and all US income documents, treaty documentation if applicable, and records of all days physically present in the US during the calendar year. Flag this requirement in the onboarding checklist and budget for professional tax preparation in the employee's relocation package.

authority: Internal Revenue Service / U.S. Department of State
deadline_label: Claim on first-year tax return; Form 8833 required for treaty positions where exempted amount exceeds $10,000
non_obvious_official_guidance: The US has income tax treaties with over 65 countries that may reduce or eliminate withholding on specific income types, provide tax residency tie-breaker rules, or exempt certain income categories during an initial period of US presence. Treaty-based positions must be disclosed on Form 8833.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Treaty benefits are frequently missed because the payroll team and the employee's tax preparer are unaware of the applicable treaty or misapply it. A common error: payroll staff claim the 'exempt individual' treaty exemption from SPT counting — which applies only to F and J visa holders — for H-1B workers, incorrectly deferring US tax residency. The reverse also occurs: employees from treaty countries (UK, France, Germany, Canada, Australia, etc.) who should claim treaty-reduced withholding rates on certain income types never do because nobody asks. Either error creates compliance exposure.
non_obvious_action_required: Before the first payroll, identify the employee's home country and check whether the US has an income tax treaty with it at irs.gov/businesses/international-businesses/united-states-income-tax-treaties-a-to-z. Have an international tax advisor review the relevant treaty articles for the employee's specific income types (wages, equity, pension). If a treaty benefit is claimed, adjust withholding via Form W-4 additional withholding fields. File Form 8833 with the annual return. Never claim F/J 'exempt individual' SPT provisions for H-1B workers — it does not apply.

authority: State Department of Revenue (varies by state)
form_name: No form — determined by state of employment
field_label: States With No Individual Income Tax
deadline_label: Effective immediately — determines whether state withholding account is needed
non_obvious_official_guidance: Nine US states impose no individual income tax on wages: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee (dividend/interest tax phased out by 2023), Texas, Washington (no tax on earned wages), Wyoming, and New Hampshire (dividend/interest tax phased out by 2025).
non_obvious_actual_reality: HR generalists managing relocations to Texas, Florida, or Washington routinely set up state withholding accounts that are legally unnecessary. More critically, employees relocating from high-tax states (California top rate 13.3%; New York top rate 10.9%) with unvested equity or deferred compensation are often surprised by an unexpected bill from their prior state — California and New York assert source-state taxation on equity and bonuses attributable to employment periods within those states, even after the employee has left. The physical move does not extinguish the prior state's claim on pre-move-vesting compensation.
non_obvious_action_required: Confirm the state of employment and residence before first payroll setup. Do not register for state withholding in AK, FL, NV, SD, TX, WA, or WY. For employees transferring from California, New York, or Massachusetts with unvested RSUs or deferred compensation, explicitly flag the source-state taxation issue and direct them to a state tax specialist — this is a material financial exposure that the employee almost never anticipates and that standard relocation advisors routinely overlook.
source: State income tax codes (e.g., Texas Tax Code — no income tax; California R&TC §17041; NY Tax Law §601)

field_label: ITIN for Dependents Not Eligible for SSN
deadline_label: Apply when filing first US tax return if dependents cannot obtain an SSN

form_name: LCA and I-129 (on file with employer)
field_label: H-1B Status Maintenance — LCA Wage Compliance
deadline_label: Continuous — required wage must be paid throughout entire H-1B employment period

form_name: Form I-129 (H amendment supplement) with new Form ETA-9035E
field_label: H-1B Amendment Required for Material Changes
deadline_label: File before the material change takes effect — no retroactive amendments
non_obvious_official_guidance: A new H-1B petition (amendment) must be filed whenever there is a 'material change' in the terms and conditions of employment approved in the original petition. Per Matter of Simeio Solutions, LLC, a new worksite outside the geographic area covered by the existing LCA constitutes a material change requiring an amended petition with a new LCA.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Remote and hybrid work expansions, promotions with significantly different job duties, office relocations to a new city or metropolitan area, and salary changes that fall below the LCA wage level all routinely trigger the H-1B amendment requirement — and the overwhelming majority of SME HR teams are unaware of this. Employees working at unamended worksites are in technical violation of their H-1B status. USCIS discovered this pattern through FDNS site visits; the consequence is a Notice of Intent to Revoke (NOIR) and a finding that the employee worked without authorization during the unamended period, which can disqualify them from future immigration benefits.
non_obvious_action_required: Establish an internal HR gate: any change in job title, material shift in job duties, compensation change, or office location change for an H-1B worker must be reviewed by immigration counsel before implementation — not after. For remote/hybrid arrangements, file a new LCA for each metropolitan statistical area (MSA) where the employee will regularly work and amend the I-129 to cover those worksites. Premium processing (I-907) is available for amendments and is advisable when the change is time-sensitive.
source: Matter of Simeio Solutions, LLC, 26 I&N Dec. 542 (AAO 2015); 8 CFR §214.2(h)(11)

authority: USCIS — Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS)
deadline_label: No advance notice — may occur at any time during authorized stay
non_obvious_official_guidance: USCIS's Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate conducts unannounced Administrative Site Visit and Verification Program (ASVVP) inspections at employer worksites to verify that petitioners are complying with the terms of approved petitions. Officers confirm the beneficiary's presence, role, and worksite.
non_obvious_actual_reality: FDNS officers arrive without notice at the employer's registered worksite address and may also visit the employee's home address listed on the petition. If the employer cannot confirm the employee's presence at the listed location, cannot produce the Public Access File, or if the employee's described duties materially differ from the petition, FDNS may recommend a Notice of Intent to Revoke. Employees who work remotely or at a client site not covered by an amended petition are particularly exposed. Receptionists who are unaware of the process sometimes make statements — 'Oh, she doesn't work here, she works from home' — that trigger a NOIR for an employee who is actually in valid status.
non_obvious_action_required: Brief all front-desk staff, building security, and direct managers that if a federal officer presents a USCIS badge and asks to verify an employee's presence or role, they should immediately contact HR and immigration counsel before making any statements. Do not instruct staff to deny entry (they are not required to allow access) but also do not allow them to improvise answers. Maintain the PAF at the worksite at all times. For hybrid and remote workers, ensure the LCA and petition reflect all regular work locations, and that the employee can demonstrate their actual duties match the petition description.
source: 8 CFR §214.1(h); USCIS FDNS Administrative Site Visit and Verification Program (ASVVP)

deadline_label: File extension petition at least 6 months before current I-94 expiry; do not let status lapse

form_name: Form I-129 (ACWIA/AC21 extension); Form I-140 (immigrant petition)
field_label: H-1B Extension Beyond 6 Years Under AC21 §106
deadline_label: 1-year extensions available if PERM or I-140 pending 365+ days; 3-year extensions if I-140 approved
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under AC21 §106 (Pub. L. 106-313), an H-1B worker who has reached the 6-year maximum may receive 1-year H-1B extensions if a PERM application or I-140 immigrant petition has been pending (unadjudicated) for 365 days or more. If an I-140 has already been approved, 3-year extensions are available regardless of how long it has been pending.
non_obvious_actual_reality: This provision is the only mechanism that allows Indian- and Chinese-born H-1B workers to remain in status during employment-based green card backlogs that run 10–50+ years for EB-2 and EB-3 categories. The critical non-obvious trap: the 365-day clock runs from the PERM filing date, not the I-140 filing date. An employer who waits until year 5 to file PERM will likely not have 365 days of PERM pendency before the 6-year cap expires, leaving the employee with no basis for extension. Most SME HR generalists have never heard of PERM and discover this requirement too late.
non_obvious_action_required: For any H-1B employee from India or China, begin a PERM feasibility assessment by year 3 of H-1B employment. File PERM no later than the start of year 5 to ensure 365 days of pendency before the year-6 cap. Track PERM filing dates in the HR system as a hard deadline, not a soft goal. For employees who qualify for EB-1A (extraordinary ability) or EB-1C (multinational manager), assess eligibility immediately — these categories require no PERM and have shorter or no backlogs, dramatically changing the timeline calculus.

deadline_label: April 15 of the following year; October 15 with automatic extension (Form 4868)

authority: State Department of Revenue (varies by state)
form_name: State income tax return (varies — e.g., CA Form 540; NY IT-201; TX — none)
deadline_label: Usually April 15; some states differ — confirm for each state of employment
source: State income tax codes (varies by state)

authority: FinCEN / U.S. Department of the Treasury
deadline_label: April 15 (auto-extended to Oct 15 if missed); reports prior calendar year
non_obvious_official_guidance: Any US person — including resident aliens who meet the Substantial Presence Test — who has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts with an aggregate value exceeding $10,000 at any point during the calendar year must file FinCEN Form 114 electronically via the BSA E-Filing System. The FBAR is filed separately from the tax return, with FinCEN — not the IRS.
non_obvious_actual_reality: H-1B and L-1 workers who become US tax residents are almost universally unaware that FBAR applies to them. An employee who simply retains a bank account in their home country — a UK current account, a French Livret A, a Canadian chequing account — may trigger the reporting obligation even if the balance is modest. After Bittner v. United States, 598 U.S. 85 (2023), non-willful penalties are assessed per report (not per account), but the amount can still reach $10,000 per year per unfiled FBAR. Willful violations carry penalties of the greater of $100,000 or 50% of account balance per year and potential criminal prosecution.
non_obvious_action_required: Include an explicit FBAR disclosure in the onboarding materials for any employee who will become a US tax resident. Do not provide tax advice — direct them to an international tax professional. Key points to convey: (1) FBAR is separate from the tax return and filed at bsaefiling.fincen.treas.gov; (2) the $10,000 threshold is aggregate across ALL foreign accounts on the same day, not per account; (3) signature authority over a company account abroad (e.g., a foreign subsidiary account the employee controlled in their home country) also triggers reporting. This obligation begins in the first year of US tax residency.
source: 31 USC §5314; 31 CFR §1010.350; Bittner v. United States, 598 U.S. 85 (2023)

form_name: Form 8938 (Statement of Specified Foreign Financial Assets)
deadline_label: Filed with annual tax return (April 15 / Oct 15 extension); single filer in US: $50k at year-end or $75k at any point
non_obvious_official_guidance: US taxpayers including resident aliens must attach Form 8938 to their annual income tax return if specified foreign financial assets exceed threshold amounts. Thresholds for a single filer residing in the US: $50,000 at year-end or $75,000 at any point during the year. Higher thresholds apply for married filing jointly and taxpayers residing abroad.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Form 8938 and the FBAR overlap but are NOT duplicates — both may need to be filed for the same accounts because reporting definitions differ. FBAR is narrower (bank and financial accounts); Form 8938 is broader and includes foreign pension plans, foreign entity interests, and certain financial instruments. Foreign employer pension plans — UK occupational pensions, French PERCOs, German betriebliche Altersversorgung, Canadian RRSPs — commonly trigger both reporting obligations simultaneously. Missing Form 8938 carries a $10,000 penalty per failure, increasing to $50,000 for continued non-compliance after IRS notice.
non_obvious_action_required: The employee must disclose all foreign financial accounts AND all foreign financial assets (including pension plans and retirement accounts) to their international tax professional upon first engagement. Key assets that are frequently missed: foreign employer-sponsored pension plans, foreign individual retirement/savings plans with tax-advantaged status in the home country, foreign life insurance policies with cash surrender value, and shareholdings in foreign private companies. Whether the home-country plan is protected by treaty from current US taxation is a separate analysis the advisor must perform.

authority: Social Security Administration / Foreign Social Security Authority
form_name: Certificate of Coverage (issued by home-country authority)
field_label: US Totalization Agreements — Avoid Double FICA
deadline_label: Request Certificate of Coverage before first payroll — cannot be applied retroactively without IRS Form 843 refund claim
non_obvious_official_guidance: The US has totalization agreements with approximately 30 countries. Under these agreements, an employee temporarily assigned to the US from a covered country may be exempt from US FICA taxes if they obtain a Certificate of Coverage from their home country's social security authority and continue contributing to the home-country system.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Most SME HR teams have never heard of totalization agreements. As a result, employees from the UK, France, Germany, Norway, the Netherlands, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and other covered countries are routinely subjected to double FICA withholding — paying into both their home-country social security system AND US Social Security and Medicare simultaneously. The exemption is legal and bilateral but requires proactive action: obtaining the Certificate of Coverage before the first paycheck. Recovering erroneously withheld FICA requires IRS Form 843 — a slow, manual refund process that can take 12–18 months and often results in partial recoveries.
non_obvious_action_required: When onboarding any work visa employee, check the SSA totalization agreements list at ssa.gov/international/agreements_overview.html against the employee's home country. If covered, confirm: (1) Is the assignment expected to be temporary (typically under 5 years)? (2) Is the employee continuing to contribute to their home country social security system? If both are yes, instruct the employee to request a Certificate of Coverage from their home country authority immediately — before the first paycheck. Provide the certificate to the payroll team to stop US FICA withholding and retain it in the HR file as documentation.
source: Social Security Act §233; 42 USC §433; SSA International Totalization Agreements

form_name: No new filing required if conditions are met (portability is self-executing)
field_label: H-1B Portability — Job Change Under AC21 §105
deadline_label: Available once I-140 approved AND I-485 pending 180+ days; new employment in same or similar SOC occupation
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under AC21 §105 (8 USC §1154(j)), an alien whose I-140 immigrant petition has been approved and whose I-485 (adjustment of status) has been pending for 180 or more days may change employers or positions without the new employer filing a new I-140, provided the new position is in the same or similar occupational classification as the original sponsored position.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Employees with I-140 approvals who are deep in the green card backlog — sometimes after 5–10 years of H-1B employment — are frequently unaware they can change employers without losing their priority date (which determines their place in the green card queue). This ignorance traps employees in jobs they would otherwise leave, particularly after restructurings or acquisitions. Employers unaware of portability may also inadvertently terminate a long-tenure H-1B employee without understanding that the employee will then port their priority date and green card case to a competitor — taking the employer's multi-year PERM investment with them.
non_obvious_action_required: Identify all H-1B employees who have an approved I-140 and an I-485 that has been pending 180+ days — these employees hold portability rights. Brief them on what portability means and what 'same or similar' occupation means (typically same 2-digit SOC major group). If contemplating RIF or restructuring, consult immigration counsel before issuing termination notices to any employee in this category. If the employee is changing jobs voluntarily and wants to use portability, the new employer should file a new I-140 as a backup, but the old I-140 approval and priority date survive.
source: AC21 §105, Pub. L. 106-313; 8 USC §1154(j); USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 7, Part A

authority: DOL Employment and Training Administration / USCIS
form_name: Form ETA-9089 (PERM) → Form I-140 → Form I-485
field_label: Green Card — PERM Labor Certification and Priority Date
deadline_label: PERM filed anytime; I-140 after approval; I-485 only when priority date is current per DOS Visa Bulletin
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employment-based permanent residence (EB-2 or EB-3) for most H-1B and L-1 workers requires: (1) DOL PERM labor certification (market test, typically 12–18 months to complete); (2) USCIS Form I-140 immigrant petition; (3) USCIS Form I-485 adjustment of status, filed only when a visa number is available per the State Department Visa Bulletin.
non_obvious_actual_reality: For India-born employees in EB-2 and EB-3 categories, DOS Visa Bulletin data as of mid-2026 shows final action dates more than 10 years in the past — meaning the effective wait in queue can exceed 10–20 years from the PERM filing date. For China-born, EB-2 wait is approximately 3–7 years. Most SME HR teams do not know that PERM must begin years before the H-1B 6-year cap to ensure the employee qualifies for AC21 extensions. Discovering this at year 5 is typically too late for Indian nationals.
non_obvious_action_required: For H-1B employees from India or China, initiate a PERM feasibility review no later than year 3 of H-1B employment. File PERM no later than the beginning of year 5 to ensure 365 days of pendency before the 6-year cap (required for AC21 §106 1-year extensions). Check whether the employee qualifies for EB-1A (extraordinary ability) or EB-1C (multinational manager/executive) — these require no PERM and have no backlog for most nationalities, making them dramatically faster. Monitor the DOS Visa Bulletin monthly and engage dedicated immigration counsel for all sponsored green card cases.
source: INA §203(b); 20 CFR Part 656 (PERM regulations); 8 CFR Part 204

form_name: No form — eligibility assessed at benefit claim time
field_label: Social Security Retirement Benefit Eligibility — 40-Quarter Requirement
deadline_label: 40 quarters of covered earnings required for eligibility; accumulates continuously during employment
non_obvious_official_guidance: To receive US Social Security retirement benefits, an individual generally needs 40 quarters of coverage (10 years of covered employment). Non-citizen non-residents who earned credits but are not residing in the US at the time of benefit claim may receive benefits depending on their country of citizenship and applicable totalization agreements (42 USC §402).
non_obvious_actual_reality: H-1B workers who pay FICA for 5–6 years — below the 40-quarter threshold — and then return to their home country receive no US Social Security retirement benefit. There is no refund mechanism for FICA contributions that do not reach the eligibility threshold. This means employees from non-totalization countries who work in the US for fewer than 10 years effectively make an irrecoverable contribution to the US Social Security system. For employees from totalization countries, home-country and US credits may be combined to reach the threshold — but only for eligibility determination, not for benefit calculation.
non_obvious_action_required: Inform employees paying FICA of the 40-quarter threshold and its implications for their personal financial planning, especially if the assignment is short-term (under 10 years). For employees from totalization countries, explain credit-totalization eligibility. For employees from non-totalization countries with assignments under 10 years, this is material financial information that affects retirement planning — they should maximize contributions to home-country retirement accounts accordingly. This is not tax advice; it is disclosure of a material fact about the FICA contributions being deducted from their paycheck.
source: Social Security Act §202; 42 USC §402; SSA Publication No. 05-10137

deadline_label: Employer plans: typically October–November for January 1 coverage; ACA marketplace: Nov 1 – Jan 15

authority: State Department of Motor Vehicles (varies by state)
field_label: Driver's License Renewal Tied to Immigration Status Expiry
deadline_label: Renew within 30 days of each H-1B (or other visa) extension approval; do not drive on expired license
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the REAL ID Act, states may issue driver's licenses to non-immigrants with limited validity matching the authorized period of stay. When the underlying immigration document is renewed or extended, the license must be renewed separately to reflect updated validity.
non_obvious_actual_reality: H-1B employees who receive an approved extension often do not realize that their driver's license — which was set to expire on the same date as their prior I-94 — has already expired or will expire imminently. Driving on an expired license is a traffic violation regardless of valid immigration status. An expired license also triggers failures in financial account verifications, background check identity layers, and TSA identity checks for domestic air travel (if no passport is available). The DMV renewal requires presenting the updated I-94 print-out and I-129 approval notice; some state DMVs have limited experience with this process and incorrectly refuse renewal without supervisor escalation.
non_obvious_action_required: Each time an H-1B (or other work visa) petition is approved for extension, immediately add a calendar task: schedule DMV renewal appointment within 30 days. Required documents: new I-94 print-out, I-129 approval notice, current passport and visa stamp, existing license. Do not let the employee drive in the gap between old and new I-94 on an expired license. Some states (e.g., California, New York) allow DMV online renewal for status extensions; most require an in-person appointment. Build this into the post-approval checklist alongside payroll and HR record updates.
source: REAL ID Act of 2005, Pub. L. 109-13, §202(c)(2)(C); state vehicle codes
